extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and extraction of the normative proposals and evaluative criteria found in Books V–VI of Plato's Republic (as presented and commented on in the excerpt). Focuses on the political, social, educational, and epistemic standards Plato advances for an ideal state and its guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community of wives and children (communal family)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal that wives and children be held in common: 'After the selection has been made, they will dwell in common houses and have their meals in common.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rulers will select partners; communal living and communal meals; avoid licentiousness by instituting 'holy marriage festivals' whose holiness correlates with usefulness; mothers will suckle children but must not recognise their own offspring; attendants handle night watch and infant care. The arrangement is enforced by law and overseen by rulers/legislators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled mating and eugenic pairing
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulers must contrive unions so that 'the good must be paired with the good, and the bad with the bad,' using 'a strong dose of falsehood' when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hymeneal festivals are timed 'with an eye to population'; an ingenious system of lots will be used to bring the brave and fair together while attributing the result to chance; offspring of the 'good' are reared, those of the 'bad' are to be destroyed. The rulers may manipulate information and events to secure desirable unions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Age limits for parents and regulated marriage timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents should be 'in the prime of life' — for men reckoned at thirty years (from twenty-five to fifty-five) and for women from twenty to forty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation in hymeneals outside specified ages is 'guilty of impiety'; marriages at other times require rulers' consent. After the specified ages individuals may 'range at will' but must avoid prohibited degrees of kinship unless dispensation is obtained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and prohibition of certain degrees of affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibited degrees (parents and children, brothers and sisters) are to be regulated despite communal arrangements: 'brothers and sisters are all such as are born seven or nine months after the espousals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kinship is defined relative to hymeneal festivals; complications arise because common living obscures natural relations. Dispensation can be procured in some cases. The text also notes practical difficulties and possible paradoxes in making this table of prohibited degrees consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common property to secure unity and prevent discord
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity is the greatest good of a State, achieved where 'there are no private pleasures or pains or interests' and 'the citizens will have all things in common.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common property produces common pleasures and pains, reduces strife (no lawsuits about property), eliminates flattery of the rich, and frees citizens from sordid household cares, borrowing, and debt. The State thereby becomes more unified and less prone to discord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military suitability of communism and youth training for war
rubrics_metrics.description: The communistic principle 'is adapted to military service'—young warriors must be trained by exposure and under veterans: 'Parents will take their children to look on at a battle... Young warriors must learn, but they must not run into danger.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training includes placing youths under experienced veterans, providing swift and tractable steeds ('wings'), teaching riding, and exposing children to appropriate examples (as potters' boys at the wheel). Risk is permitted only insofar as benefit warrants it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewards and honours for bravery
rubrics_metrics.description: Brave warriors receive public honours and tangible rewards: 'he shall be crowned by all the youths... receive the right hand of fellowship... be kissed... have more wives... have more to eat... be worshipped after death.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honours include public crown, fellowship, preferential seating/food at feasts (Homeric 'long chines'), reproductive privileges (more wives) to produce many children, and posthumous cultic honours (admission to golden race / guardian angels). These incentives promote martial virtue and procreation of the brave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for cowardice and desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Cowards and deserters face degradation: 'Cowards and deserters shall be degraded to the class of husbandmen; gentlemen who allow themselves to be taken prisoners, may be presented to the enemy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military failure has social and occupational penalties designed to deter cowardice. By demoting or humiliating those who fail courage tests, the State enforces martial discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of warfare and treatment of enemies
rubrics_metrics.description: Constraints on conduct in war: do not enslave fellow Hellenes, do not despoil the dead, limit devastation (don't burn houses or carry off more than annual produce), and distinguish civil from foreign war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: War between Hellenes is 'civil' and should aim at reconciliation; action should be constrained to punitive measures against guilty persons rather than wholesale subjugation of peoples. Ritual pollution (e.g., offering arms of Hellenes in temples) should be avoided. These principles place ethical limits on military conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers as rulers (necessity of philosopher-kings)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Until kings are philosophers, or philosophers are kings, cities will never cease from ill' — philosophers should be chosen as rulers if they possess other required qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophers, by having knowledge of true being and patterns of justice/beauty/truth, are the appropriate leaders. The claim is both normative (they should rule) and explanatory (their rule is necessary for the ideal polity). Practical obstacles are acknowledged (few philosophers, corruption, resistance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities required in philosopher-rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers are 'lovers of the knowledge of the eternal and of all truth; they are haters of falsehood; their meaner desires are absorbed in the interests of knowledge... social, gracious disposition, equally free from cowardice and arrogance... learn and remember easily; they have harmonious, well-regulated minds.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These dispositions and cognitive capacities (love of truth, hatred of falsehood, self-mastery, social grace, memory, harmony of soul) are necessary conditions for ruling wisely. The text warns that possessing these in practice is rare and that corruption is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnosis of corruption risks for philosophers
rubrics_metrics.description: Many causes tend to 'destroy' the philosopher: public opinion, sophists, flattery, exile or death, social soil unsuited to rare natures, and worldly temptations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even well-disposed philosophers can be ruined by unsuitable social environments; the 'hireling Sophist' flatters public opinion and corrupts youth. Education and social structures must protect philosophers from these corrupting influences if they are to rule rightly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper education and testing of guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must be 'lovers of their country' and be 'tested in the refiner's fire of pleasures and pains' and in 'the highest branches of knowledge'; they must not faint in the search after truth and must be prepared to take the longer road (dialectic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should include moral testing via exposure to pleasures/pain, rigorous intellectual training (dialectic), and attainment of clear and distinct vision of higher truths (including the idea of the Good). The sequence of education is important and demanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct order and method for philosophic education (dialectic emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The present mode of study is criticized; 'the real difficulty, which is dialectic,' must be mastered. The recommended order: begin with gymnastics in youth, increase 'gymnastics of the soul' as the man strengthens, and finally return to philosophy after active life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialectic is the central skill; superficial or intermittent study (occasional lectures) is inadequate. Education must be systematic: bodily training in youth, cultivation of the soul, and concentrated philosophical study culminating in dialectic capable of grasping the Good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of knowledge of the Good for rulers
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea of the Good is 'the sun of intelligent natures,' 'the cause of knowledge and truth,' and is required for real knowledge of anything; guardians should not be ignorant of this supreme principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good is more than wisdom or pleasure; it is the highest principle analogous to the sun in the visible realm. Rulers must apprehend it (not merely opinion) because knowledge of the Good underpins correct judgment and governance. The text admits difficulty in fully describing the Good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive taxonomy and stages of knowledge (visible vs intelligible)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-world division (visible and intelligible) and a fourfold subdivision (shadows/reflections; real objects in the visible; mathematics; dialectic ascent to the idea of Good) describes stages of cognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education must move the soul from the lesser realms of sense and opinion (shadows, reflections) through objects and mathematical hypothesis, and finally by dialectic to grasp the intelligible and the Good. Mathematical reasoning is treated as a preparatory 'division' useful as hypotheses but not final; dialectic uses those hypotheses to ascend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artifice of rulers and use of noble falsehoods
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers may need 'a strong dose of falsehood' and to 'ascribe to chance what is really the invention of the rulers' to manage social relations and secure desirable outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deceptive practices (myths, engineered lots, controlled narratives) are morally sanctioned as political technologies to maintain order, effect selection, and preserve unity. The text treats such falsehoods as tools to be used by skilful 'physicians of the State' when necessary.
